Could you tell me whether the Moon would be visible to me at the moment?

I'm in Cairo, Egypt at 2026-12-14 18:03 EET (UTC+0200) (2026-12-14T16:03:00Z in UTC), at latitude 30.0444 degrees and longitude 31.2357 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -13.537 degrees and its azimuth is 251.05 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 37.398 degrees and its azimuth is 217.264 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 25.89 percent illuminated, 61.039 degrees from the Sun, and 397433.2 kilometers away. The sky brightness is astronomical twilight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes — very likely.

At your time and location, the Moon is about **37° above the horizon** in the **southwest** (azimuth ~217°), which is a comfortably high position. It is a **25.9%-illuminated crescent**, so it will not be as conspicuous as a half or full Moon, but it should still be readily visible to normal unaided eyesight under a clear sky.

The main limiting factor is that the Sun is only **13.5° below the horizon**, during **astronomical twilight**. The sky will still retain some residual brightness, especially toward the western/southwestern sky where the Moon lies and only about **61° from the Sun**. That reduces contrast somewhat.

Still, with a clear view and knowing where to look, you should be able to spot it. Look roughly **southwest**, about **two-thirds of the way from the horizon to overhead**. It may appear as a fairly thin but distinct bright crescent rather than a dramatic, obvious Moon at first glance.

It should become progressively easier to see as twilight deepens over the next several tens of minutes.
